title: The Nature of Science and Physics
learning_objectives: Explain what physics studies and how it connects to technology, medicine and the other sciences.
Distinguish a model, a theory and a law, and describe the role of experiment in deciding whether a theory stands.
Identify the SI base units and use metric prefixes to express physical quantities.
Convert quantities between units using dimensional analysis.
Report measurements with the correct accuracy, precision and significant figures, and make order-of-magnitude estimates.
no_formula_reason: This chapter teaches measurement and the language of physics. It introduces no physical law of its own.

definition.text: The systematic study of the natural world through observation, experiment and reasoning.
The branch of science that studies matter, energy, motion, forces and the rules that connect them.
A simplified representation of a system that is used to make predictions.
A well-tested explanation of a set of observations that can be revised when new evidence appears.
A statement that describes a regular relationship in nature, often in mathematical form.
A testable proposed explanation for an observation.
A controlled procedure that tests a hypothesis or a prediction.
A unit in the International System of Units, the agreed base for scientific measurement.
A unit formed by combining base units, such as the newton or the joule.
A prefix that scales a unit by a power of ten, such as kilo or milli.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
How closely repeated measurements agree with one another.
The range within which a measured value is likely to lie.
The digits in a measurement that carry meaningful information about its precision.
A value or answer that is close enough for its purpose, often found by rounding or estimating.
The nearest power of ten to a quantity.

sections.title: Introduction to the Nature of Science and Physics
objectives: Describe how physics connects to technology, other sciences and everyday life.
summary: Physics studies the fundamental laws of nature, from particles to galaxies.
Those laws underlie technology, medicine, engineering and the other sciences.

sections.title: Physics: An Introduction
objectives: Explain how physics relates to other sciences and to technology.
Distinguish a model, a theory and a law, and describe how experiment tests them.

misconceptions.claim: A scientific law is a theory that has been proved.
misconceptions.correction: A law describes a regular relationship, often as an equation. A theory explains why the relationship holds. Neither is proved beyond revision; both are tested against experiment.
misconceptions.signal: The word law sounds like a final verdict. In science it is not.

misconceptions.claim: A model is just a guess.
misconceptions.correction: A model is a deliberate simplification. It can be physical, mathematical or computational, and it is judged by how well it predicts.
misconceptions.signal: The everyday meaning of model is a person or a small copy. In physics it is a working representation.

summary: Physics is the study of matter, energy, motion and the forces that connect them.
Models simplify a system, theories explain observations, and laws describe regular relationships.
Experiment decides whether a model or theory stands. A failed prediction forces a revision.

authored_exercises.stem: In one sentence, state the difference between a scientific model and a scientific theory.
authored_exercises.answer: A model is a simplified representation used to make predictions; a theory is a well-tested explanation that can be revised.
solution: A model simplifies a system so that its behaviour can be predicted.
A theory explains a broad set of observations and is tested against experiment. It is not a guess, and it can be revised.

authored_exercises.stem: A theory predicts that a new particle will decay in a certain way. An experiment finds a different decay pattern. What should happen to the theory, and why?
authored_exercises.answer: It must be revised or replaced, because experiment decides whether a theory stands.
solution: A theory is tested by its predictions.
When a prediction fails, the theory cannot be kept unchanged.
The theory is revised or replaced by one that fits the evidence.

authored_exercises.stem: A model of a bridge treats the bridge as a perfectly rigid beam. Give one situation in which this model is useful and one in which it fails.
authored_exercises.answer: Useful when the bridge bends only slightly under normal loads; it fails when the bridge bends a lot, vibrates, or breaks.
solution: The rigid-beam model is useful when deformation is small compared with the bridge's size.
It fails when deformation, vibration or failure matters, because those depend on the bridge's elasticity and structure.

sections.title: Physical Quantities and Units
objectives: Identify the SI base units for length, mass and time, and use metric prefixes.
Convert quantities between units using dimensional analysis.

misconceptions.claim: A number is a complete physical quantity even without a unit.
misconceptions.correction: A physical quantity needs a number and a unit. The unit gives the number meaning and allows comparison.
misconceptions.signal: Answers that drop the unit look complete but cannot be checked.

misconceptions.claim: Changing a metric prefix changes the size of the quantity.
misconceptions.correction: A prefix changes the unit, not the physical quantity. 1 km and 1000 m describe the same length.
misconceptions.signal: A larger number with a smaller unit can describe the same length.

summary: SI base units give scientists a common language for length, mass, time and other quantities.
Metric prefixes scale a unit by powers of ten without changing the physical quantity.
Dimensional analysis converts units by multiplying by ratios equal to one.

sections.title: Accuracy, Precision, and Significant Figures
objectives: Distinguish accuracy from precision and explain what uncertainty means.
Report calculated results with the correct number of significant figures.

misconceptions.claim: A precise measurement is always accurate.
misconceptions.correction: Precision is agreement among repeated measurements. Accuracy is closeness to the true value. A precise set can be consistently wrong.
misconceptions.signal: Repeated readings that agree feel trustworthy, even when the instrument is wrongly calibrated.

misconceptions.claim: More significant figures always means a better measurement.
misconceptions.correction: Significant figures show the precision of the instrument and the measurement. Digits beyond that precision are not meaningful.
misconceptions.signal: A calculator can show many digits, but the instrument cannot support them.

summary: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is agreement among repeated measurements.
Uncertainty states the range within which a measured value is likely to lie.
A calculated result is reported with the number of significant figures supported by the measurements.

authored_exercises.stem: How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.00450 m?
solution: The digits 4, 5 and the trailing zero after the decimal point are significant.

sections.title: Approximation
objectives: Make order-of-magnitude estimates using simple arithmetic.
Explain when an approximation is appropriate and when it is not.

misconceptions.correction: An approximation is a reasoned estimate built from known quantities and simple arithmetic. A guess has no stated basis.
misconceptions.signal: The word approximate is often read as careless. In physics it is a controlled estimate.

misconceptions.claim: An order-of-magnitude answer is useless because it is not exact.
misconceptions.correction: An order-of-magnitude answer checks whether an exact answer is plausible and catches large errors in units or powers of ten.
misconceptions.signal: An exact-looking answer can still be wrong by a factor of a thousand.

summary: An approximation is a reasoned estimate, not a guess.
Order-of-magnitude estimates use powers of ten and simple arithmetic.
Approximations check whether an exact answer is plausible and expose large errors.

authored_exercises.stem: Estimate the number of seconds in one day to the nearest order of magnitude.
solution: The nearest power of ten is 10^5 s.
